cues.zh: 从南到北，从东到西，我们遍布全球。我们去了北极，去了复活节岛，而这一切基本上都没有文字记载。我们是怎么做到的？那些在极端环境下生存繁衍所需的极高技能，我们到底是如何传承的？答案就是口述交流。我们靠说，也靠听。

cues.en: And this is very, very, very deep in our animal brain, I believe. This is a survival skill that we have. The ability to convey, to tell stories, and to listen. So this is very, very deep. cues.en: And of course, now I'm going to turn that on. And of course, yes, Mr. Dialog can be turned by Mac. But this is amazing. This is amazing that this has survived. cues.zh: 当然，现在我要把它打开。当然，是的，Mr. Dialog 也能被 Mac 打开。但这太神奇了。这太神奇了，这东西居然流传下来了。就算我们想，也没法把它从孩子们脑子里根除。顺便问一句，这是从哪来的？其实我们并不知道。它出现在 60 年代。有人推测，军队高层是这种特殊“疾病”的传播媒介。

cues.en: But honestly, we're not going to care enough to figure it out, and we might as well just get comfortable with it, because Jingle Bell's Batman Smells is going to be with us until the end of days, and it will survive the apocalypse. But this is amazing, right? That oral tradition. You heard that from somebody, you probably said it to somebody else, and now our kids and their kids and their kids and their kids will be singing this little jingle. And this shows this incredible power, and it also plays a role, a very important role, in software engineering.
cues.zh: 但说实话，我们不会真在意到去把它弄清楚，倒不如直接习惯它，因为《Jingle Bells, Batman Smells》会一直陪着我们，直到世界末日，也会在末日之后存活下来。但这很神奇，对吧？这种口头传统。你从某个人那里听到，可能又对另一个人说了，现在我们的孩子、孩子的孩子、再下一代会一直唱这首小调。这展现了惊人的力量，而它在软件工程中也扮演着非常重要角色。

cues.en: So I want to go through a little bit of a history of oral tradition of software engineering, how it's changed a lot, and where I feel it's going. In the beginning, software was totally subservient to hardware. So we actually don't know very much about early software engineering because so little was thought of it. It was held in such low regard. It was the actual building of the machines that was the thing. We didn't even really understand what it meant to build software.
cues.zh: 所以我想稍微梳理一下软件工程的口头传统史，它发生了很大变化，以及我觉得它会走向哪里。起初，软件完全从属于硬件。所以我们对早期软件工程其实了解不多，因为当时几乎没人重视它。它被看得非常低。真正重要的是造机器。我们甚至不太理解“构建软件”意味着什么。

cues.en: We didn't even call it software. We didn't even call it software in the earliest, earliest days. They didn't even call computers in the earliest days. These are accounting machines. So we actually don't have a lot, and it is true, true oral tradition. And much of it was simply not passed down. It was very proprietary, and much of it we just don't have. There are lots of architectures that were developed. We don't know anything about the software that was developed for them.
cues.zh: 我们甚至不叫它软件。最早最早的时候，我们根本不叫它软件。最早的时候，人们甚至不叫它们计算机。这些是会计机器。所以我们确实没有多少资料，这是真真正正的口头传统。其中很多根本没有传下来。它非常专有，很多我们都找不到了。当时开发过很多架构，但我们完全不知道为它们开发的软件是什么样。

cues.en: One of my favorite examples of this, I like to collect old computer manuals, and I bought a stock of old manuals, and in the manuals was a quick reference manual that I had not ordered, which is kind of in there, for a language called Language H. Language H, which I've not heard of, Language H was developed by NCR. It was actually developed by Ellyiot on the UK. It's a cobalt derivative, and it's crazy, absolutely crazy.
cues.zh: 我最喜欢的例子之一：我喜欢收集旧计算机手册，我买了一批旧手册，里面有一本我没订过的快速参考手册，就在那堆里，讲一门叫 Language H 的语言。Language H，我从没听说过；Language H 是 NCR 开发的。其实最早是英国的 Ellyiot 开发的。它是 COBOL 的衍生语言，而且很疯狂，绝对疯狂。

cues.en: Every language H program begins with chapter one. And you're like, oh, by the way, everything is in caps. This entire language is screened. So everything must be screened. So chapter one, that is the beginning of every language H program. And you're like, OK, I get it, I get it, I get it. So it's like, computer's a book. OK, I get it. It's early in software, like the metaphors of book, metaphors of literature, I get it. But then it ends with, every language H program must end with the keyword,
cues.zh: 每个 Language H 程序都以第一章开头。你会想，哦，顺便说一句，所有内容都是大写。整个语言都是以大写书写的，所以所有东西都必须大写。第一章，就是每个 Language H 程序的开头。你会说，好，我懂了，我懂了，我懂了。所以它就像，计算机是一本书。好，我懂，早期软件里就是有书、文学的隐喻，我懂。但接着它结尾是：每个 Language H 程序都必须以这个关键字结束，

cues.en: OK!
cues.zh: OK！

cues.en: Okay, it's like a book that you've been slaved? I mean, it's a very strange, it's totally mixed metaphor, the language is, and we would, I mean, and in every body of software that I've developed, there's a language HTTP strike in there somewhere, because I think this language is so peculiar and strange, and the question that I'm dying to know, and if anyone in humanity is granted omniscience, please don't let it be me, because I will waste our shot at doing something truly valuable, because if I were granted one question that I could know the answer to, that one question may be,
cues.zh: 好吧，这就像一本你被奴役的书？我是说，这比喻很奇怪，完全混淆了，这门语言是，而且我们，我是说，在我开发的每一个软件体系里，某处都会有一个语言 HTTP 的痕迹，因为我觉得这门语言太奇特、太古怪了，而我极度渴望知道的一个问题是——如果全人类中有人被赋予全知能力，请千万别是我，因为我会白白浪费掉做真正有价值事情的机会——因为如果我能被允许知道一个问题的答案，那一个问题可能会是：

cues.en: Was any software ever written in language age? And does any of that software survive today? Is there any language age running in production anywhere? I don't know. And I'd say I would burn my omniscience on that question, so you hope I don't get that opportunity. And that would be very, very, very early days of software. We still have a lot of information, unfortunately. If you want to kind of get a compendium of that oral tradition, there's a book on your bookshelf that you haven't read called The Mythical Man month. Maybe you have read it.
cues.zh: 到底有没有软件是用 H 语言写的？其中有没有任何软件幸存至今？现在还有任何 H 语言在生产环境中运行吗？我不知道。我敢说我会把我的全知机会浪费在这个问题上，所以你们最好祈祷我别得到这种机会。那可真是软件非常、非常、非常早期的时代了。可惜的是，我们现在仍有大量信息。如果你想了解那种口头传统的汇编，你的书架上有本你还没读过的书，叫《人月神话》（The Mythical Man-Month）。也许你读过。

cues.en: The reason I think that people read it, they would take it out of the undergraduate curriculum. That's why I think that people haven't read it. Because the mythical man month, there are elements, there are nuggets of real greatness in there, but it is basically extremely old fashioned and it dates from an extremely early era in software. You can drag some things into the modern era, but a lot of that just does not make sense at all.
cues.zh: 我认为人们读过它的原因是，它被移出了本科课程。所以我才觉得大家其实没读过。因为在《人月神话》里，确实有一些闪光点，有一些真正伟大的真知灼见，但它基本上极其过时，源自软件极早期的一个时代。你可以把其中的一些东西套用到现代，但很多内容根本就讲不通了。

cues.en: It's very, very, very water falling. It is, and it's very early. It's talking about System 360. It's talking about a bunch of things that we have. I mean, second system syndrome is not something that actually really exists, I would argue. And there are lots of things in there that are just, that just don't make sense. But the Mythical Man month does capture the zeitgeist of that kind of era. So it is kind of a compendium of the world tradition, not regarding it. So, which is, it's, it's valuable certainly. So, and this is where, and by the way, if you're an academic booklorist,
cues.zh: 它非常、非常、非常瀑布模型。确实如此，而且时代非常早。它讨论的是 System 360，讨论的是一大堆我们现在的……我的意思是，我觉得“第二系统综合征”其实并不是真正存在的东西。里面有很多东西就是完全站不住脚的。但《人月神话》确实捕捉到了那个时代的时代精神。所以它算是口头传统的一种汇编，并没有忽视它。这当然很有价值。所以，顺便提一下，如果你是一位学院派民俗学者，

So when oral tradition, when we take oral tradition and make it reliable, where oral tradition is actually conveying a real narrative, folklorists are called
cues.zh: 这听起来不太可能，但你也知道这是个持续一个月的活动，也不至于完全不可能。就像有人说：“不，我邀请了三位学院派民俗学者，其中一位来得了。”所以如果你是位学院派民俗学者，正感到有点反胃恶心，请多包涵我一下。我要稍微滥用一下这些术语，不过是以我认为具有建设性的方式。所以当口头传统——当我们让口头传统变得可靠，当口头传统实际上在传达一个真实叙事时，民俗学者称之为

I think that you have literature that I think should be called oral literature because it's actually meant to be spoken. It was originally spoken. It was originally heard. And now we just happen to have written it down. We happen to have recorded it. But it is fundamentally oral tradition in nature. It becomes oral literature. And for us in software engineering, oral literature exploded on Usenet. Usenet, I'm getting a little bit nervous because you dropped Bill and Ted's reference and it's like,
cues.zh: 口头文学。而且我认为口头文学是可以被写下来的。我认为有些文学作品应该被称为口头文学，因为它们本来就是要说出来的。它们最初是被讲出来的，最初是被听到的。而现在我们碰巧把它们写了下来，碰巧记录了下来。但从本质上讲，它们依然是口头传统。它就变成了口头文学。而对我们软件工程界来说，口头文学是在 Usenet 上爆发的。说到 Usenet，我有点紧张了，因为你刚刚提到了《阿比和阿弟的冒险》（Bill and Ted），感觉

Actually, I do think that one of the things that we are doing badly, I mean, Stephen asked, like, what are the things we can improve?
cues.zh: 我知道台下有足够多的人年纪大到经历过 Usenet。对于没经历过的人，Usenet 是人们早期在互联网上交流的一种方式，在新闻组里，有人发帖，其他人回复，诸如此类。这简直是有史以来对 Usenet 最差劲的解释了。算了，去查查吧。但 Usenet 上有大量有趣的东西。事实上，我确实认为我们做得很差的事情之一——我是说，Stephen 问过，我们有哪些方面可以改进？

The Usenet searching is excruciating, and we would all be well served if we could actually search Usenet well, because if you go to try to find something open on Usenet, it's very, very painful. Anyway, there's a lot of interesting stuff on Usenet, a lot of really interesting stuff.
cues.zh: 我们现在对 Usenet 真的很不上心。Usenet 的搜索体验糟透了，要是真能好好搜一下 Usenet，对大家都会很有帮助，因为现在要想在 Usenet 上找点公开内容，简直太痛苦了。不管怎么说，Usenet 上其实有很多有趣的东西，真的非常多。

cues.en: A lot of embarrassing stuff, too. I definitely put my hand high in the air on that one. There's a lot of kind of humiliating stuff on Usenet, because we didn't realize this was all going to be reported forever. But there's a lot of interesting stuff on Usenet, too. And there's a lot of kind of oral literature on Usenet that didn't quite survive, that didn't quite cross the Jingle Bell's Got Namsnow's kind of line. But one did.
cues.zh: 也有很多让人尴尬的事。对此我绝对举双手赞成。Usenet 上有很多挺丢人的黑历史，因为我们当时根本没想到这些全都会被永久记录下来。但 Usenet 上也有很多非常有趣的东西。Usenet 上还有很多类似口头文学的内容没能流传下来，没能像《铃儿响叮当》或《蝙蝠侠被雪埋》那样深入人心。但有一篇留下来了。

cues.en: And one story from Usenet has not only survived, but it has become the epic, the ur-epic, the saga of software engineering. This is penned by Ed Nather. And how many people recognize this? OK, so this is the story of NELP. And the way it begins...
cues.zh: 而 Usenet 上的一个故事不仅流传了下来，甚至成了软件工程史上的史诗、鼻祖级史诗和传奇。这篇由 Ed Nather 撰写。有多少人认得这个？好，这就是 NELP 的故事。它的开篇是这样的……

cues.en: I mean, it begins almost, it begins in the fashion of a saga. You know, real programmers, it's said that real programmers write in Fortran, maybe they do now in this decadent era of light beer, hand calculators and user-friendly software, and you're like, wait, what era is this? Of course, this is written.
cues.zh: 我的意思是，这开头简直，简直就像一部英雄传奇。大家都知道，真正的程序员——据说真正的程序员都用 Fortran 写代码，也许在这个充斥着淡啤、手持计算器和用户友好型软件的颓废时代，他们确实如此。你可能会想：等等，这是什么年代？当然，这是写出来的。

cues.en: The decadent era of light beer, I don't think, I don't know if you've commonly heard of the early 80s that way, but the decadent era of light beer, as it turns out, is 1983. But back in the good old days, when the term software sounded funny, and real computers were made out of drums and vacuum tubes, real programmers wrote in machine code. Not Fortran, not Bat4, not even assembly language. Machine code, raw, unadorned, inscrutable, hexadecimal numbers.
cues.zh: 淡啤酒的颓废时代，我想，我不知道大家是不是常听到有人这样形容80年代初，但事实证明，淡啤酒的颓废时代正是1983年。不过回到那段美好的旧时光，那时“软件”这个词听起来还很滑稽，真正的计算机还是由磁鼓和真空管组成的，真正的程序员都用机器码来写程序。不是用 Fortran，不是用 Bat4，甚至不是用汇编语言。而是机器码，原始、质朴、难以捉摸的十六进制数字。

cues.en: Directly. I mean, the writing here is so good. I mean, directly as a sentence. I mean, God, it's beautiful. The writing is amazing. And then we meet our epic hero. And again, I think that this is as much a tribute. This is an amazing story written about an amazing person, Mel Kay, by an amazing writer, Ed Navin. And lest a whole new generation of programmers grow up in ignorance of this glorious past.
cues.zh: 就这一个词。我是说，这里的文笔太棒了。我是说，“直接”单独成句。天哪，写得真美。文笔太绝了。接着，我们的史诗主角登场了。再次说明，我觉得这同样是一份致敬。这是一个了不起的故事，由了不起的作家 Ed Navin，写一位了不起的人物 Mel Kay。免得新一代的程序员长大后，对这段辉煌的过去一无所知。

cues.en: I feel duty-bound to describe, as best as I can, through the generation gap, how a real programmer wrote code. I'll call him Mel, because that was his name. Oh, god, it's amazing. So good. And it's so good. And I truly mean this. This is our Iliad. This is absolutely our Iliad. This will be read in a thousand years. I say that, not in jest.
cues.zh: 我觉得自己有责任跨越时代的代沟，尽可能讲清楚一个真正的程序员是如何写代码的。我叫他 Mel，因为这就是他的名字。天呐，简直绝了。太棒了。真的太棒了。我是认真的。这就是我们的《伊利亚特》。这绝对是我们的《伊利亚特》。千年之后人们依然会读它。我说真的，绝无戏言。

cues.en: This will be right in a thousand years. And one of the things I love about this is the way this is formatted, by the way, where the lines are, this is formatted because of how it was handed around Usenet. This is, no one knows what the original formatting was, but it wasn't this. This was just like, as people are like, quoting it, handing around it, transcribing it, this is what it ended up being. So it has this kind of, this Homeric feel to it.
cues.zh: 千年之后这也依然成立。顺便说一句，我特别喜欢它的一点就是排版，比如换行的位置，现在的排版是因为它当年在 Usenet 上被四处转帖导致的。没人知道最初的排版是什么样，但绝不是现在这样。这只是大家在不断引用、转发、抄录的过程中，最终演变成的模样。所以它自带一种荷马史诗般的质感。

cues.en: And the story, those of you who don't know, the story about Mel K, again, it's a true story. Mel K is a programmer for a company called Leberscope, they made an LGP-30. And the Leberscope was a drum-based machine. So a drum-based machine, this is very, very early computing. So the IBM 650, which is, IBM 650 is the first really...
cues.zh: 对于还不了解的人，这个关于 Mel K 的故事，再次重申，是个真人真事。Mel K 是 Librascope 公司的程序员，他们生产了 LGP-30。而 Librascope 是一台基于磁鼓的机器。基于磁鼓的机器，这属于极其早期的计算时代了。比如 IBM 650，IBM 650 实际上是第一台真正的……

cues.en: It's an accounting machine that we would really think of as the first computer. And the 650 is a drum-based machine, so everything is stored on a drum that is moving at a fixed velocity. And the way these drum-based machines would work is you would execute an instruction, and it's called one plus one addresses. So you'd execute an instruction, and in that instruction is the next address to execute. Now, so that is to say every instruction has an embedded gosu. But there's a very good reason for that.
cues.zh: 它原本是一台会计机，但我们确实把它视作第一台计算机。650 就是一台磁鼓机，所有数据都存储在一个以恒定速度旋转的磁鼓上。这些磁鼓机的工作原理是，你执行一条指令，它被称为“1+1 地址”。也就是说你执行一条指令，该指令内部就包含了下一条要执行的指令地址。所以说，每条指令都自带一个嵌入式的 goto。但这么做是有非常充分的理由的。

cues.en: because instructions take a variable length of time to execute, and you want to be sure that the drum is coming around when it's time to execute the next instruction. So you would develop something called an optimizing assembler, which would go over your code and generate the optimal
cues.zh: 因为每条指令的执行耗时各不相同，你必须确保下一条指令正好转到磁头下方时，就是该执行它的时候。所以你会开发一种叫“优化汇编器”的东西，它会通读你的代码，并生成最优的

cues.en: addressing such that it would execute literally. And this could make a huge difference in performance. Don Cuse, by the way, Don Cuse's undergraduate thesis was on writing and optimizing a semboard from the LGB650. This is not the LGB650, it's the LGB30. And this is the story of how Mel K was porting a Blackjack program from the LGB30 to the Royal McBee. I love Royal McBee.
cues.zh: 寻址方案，好让程序能即时顺畅执行。这对性能会产生天壤之别。顺便提一句，Don Knuth 的本科毕业论文写的就是为 IBM 650 编写优化汇编器。不过我们说的不是 IBM 650，而是 LGP-30。这个故事讲的就是 Mel K 如何把一个二十一点游戏程序从 LGP-30 移植到 Royal McBee 上。我超喜欢 Royal McBee

cues.en: as a name. In fact, when I first met my wife, I told her the story, she married me anyway. She's a PhD literature, she's got nothing to do with the beauty. But I said, you know, I so want us to have a cat named Royal McBee. And it took us like 15 years to do it. Well, you actually do have a cat now named Royal McBee. We just took him to the vet and you got Royal McBee cancer on there. I'm just like, oh god.
cues.zh: 这个名字。事实上，刚认识我妻子时我就跟她讲过这个故事，她还是嫁给了我。她是文学博士，跟计算机毫无关系。但我当时说，你知道吗，我好想养一只叫 Royal McBee 的猫。结果我们花了大概 15 年才实现。好吧，现在我们确实有了一只叫 Royal McBee 的猫。我们刚带它去看过兽医，单子上写着 Royal McBee 癌症，我当时心里直呼，天哪。

cues.en: I can feel like, you know, the ghost of Mel K. But so he was porting the LGB32 to this royal position, the RPC4000. And the story is about a blackout program that he's been instructed to let the customer win. And Mel's got a bug where instead of letting the customer win when a switch is enabled, it always wins. The computer always cheats and always wins. And the customer never wins. Mel views this as beautiful. Ed Nather goes in to...
cues.zh: 我隐约能感觉到，懂吧，Mel K 的幽灵在游荡。话说回来，他当时正把 LGP-30 的程序移植到这台皇家机器上，也就是 RPC-4000。故事讲的是一个二十一点程序，他接到的要求是得让顾客能赢。但 Mel 的代码有个 bug，开关打开时本该让顾客赢，结果却变成了电脑必胜。电脑总是在作弊并且总是赢，顾客永远赢不了。Mel 觉得这简直太优美了。随后 Ed Nather 跑去……

cues.en: and finds a beautiful, beautiful optimization that Mel K has made. So, that's the kind of the story, but the content of the story almost doesn't matter. It matters that it is so technically, it's technically beautiful, but it's also got all these kind of managerial aspects to it, where they've been ordered to make the program do something that the programmers think is fundamentally wrong, then the program doesn't behave in that way, and the programmers do that as fundamentally righteous. It's just beautiful.
cues.zh: 并发现了 Mel K 做的一个非常非常漂亮的优化。所以故事大概就是这样，但故事内容几乎不重要。重要的是它在技术上如此——技术上很漂亮，但它也带有所有这些管理层面的东西：他们被命令让程序做程序员认为根本错误的事，然后程序并没有按那种方式运行，而程序员这么做又是出于根本上的正义。这太美了。

cues.en: It's just beautiful. And every young software engineer will read this and aspire to be Mel K. And Mel K has passed away and Nather has passed away. So this is very prophetic. This is actually reaching out in an actual literal sense. I can't imagine that Nather meant this as literal when he wrote it.
cues.zh: 这太美了。每个年轻软件工程师读到它，都会渴望成为 Mel K。而 Mel K 已经去世，Nather 也已经去世。所以这非常有预言性。这实际上是在字面意义上触达了新一代。我无法想象 Nather 写它时本意是字面如此。

cues.en: When he wrote this, and by the way, I don't know where, this is not originally contributed to the net.jokes on May 13, 1981 or 1983, whatever it is, the Wikipedia article is wrong. I don't know where this first appeared when he used that. But when it first appeared on Usenet, he wrote this as a joke. He did not intend this to be actually reaching a new generation of programmers. But that is what it has done.
cues.zh: 他写这个的时候——顺便说，我不知道是在哪里，这不是最初在 1981 年还是 1983 年 5 月 13 日投稿到 net.jokes 的，随便哪年吧，维基百科那篇文章是错的。我不知道他第一次用这个时它首次出现在哪里。但当它首次出现在 Usenet 上时，他写这个只是当作玩笑。他并不打算让它真正触达新一代程序员。但它确实做到了。

cues.en: And it's amazing. So the story of Mel is kind of our first example, the Ur example of a beautiful oral tradition written down, becoming oral literature. And then I would say kind of the second milestone. I mean, if Mel is, the story of Mel is our Iliad, then Tracy Kidder's Soul of the New Machine has to be considered our Odyssey. How do you have read Soul of the New Machine? So Soul of the New Machine is an absolute must read.
cues.zh: 这很惊人。所以 Mel 的故事算是我们的第一个例子，是一个优美的口述传统被写下来、变成口头文学的最早范例。然后我会说，第二个里程碑。我的意思是，如果 Mel——Mel 的故事是我们的《Iliad》，那么 Tracy Kidder 的 Soul of the New Machine 就得算是我们的《Odyssey》。你读过 Soul of the New Machine 吗？所以 Soul of the New Machine 绝对必读。

cues.en: His literature, it is Tracy Fitter, who's an unbelievably beautiful writer, terrific, terrific writer, who sat with Data General as they were building a new computer and watched the whole process, warts and all. And this is not, it's more complicated than a heroic story. There's a reason why, it's the Odyssey.
cues.zh: 他的文学——是 Tracy Fitter，一位美得难以置信的作家，非常非常出色的作家，他和 Data General 坐在一起，看他们造一台新电脑，全程观察，毫不美化。而这并不是——它比英雄故事更复杂。它之所以是《Odyssey》，是有原因的。

cues.en: and not the Gilead. It is, Odysseus is a complicated, Tom West in this case, is a complicated figure, and he deliberately tortures his team to get them to produce what he thinks are higher results. But it's an incredibly good read. It remains very, very important.
cues.zh: 而不是 Gilead。它是——Odysseus 是个复杂人物，在这个例子里，Tom West 是个复杂人物，他故意折磨团队，逼他们产出他认为更高的成果。但它读起来极其过瘾。它仍然非常非常重要。

cues.en: So if you read Soul of the New Machine, if you read Soul, I imagine you'd agree with this, that Soul of the New Machine still has relevance for us today. And you will find shadows of yourself in it today, maybe shadows of your manager in it today. But Soul of the New Machine is an absolute must-read. And again, it's kind of entered our lore, and rightfully so. So these two, I think, are kind of the classics.
cues.zh: 所以如果你读过 Soul of the New Machine，如果你读过 Soul，我想你会同意：Soul of the New Machine 今天对我们仍然有意义。今天你会在其中看到自己的影子，也许还会看到你经理的影子。但 Soul of the New Machine 绝对必读。再说一次，它算是进入了我们的传说，而且理所当然。所以我认为，这两部算是经典。

cues.en: In the 80s and 90s, the older I get, the more certain I am of this. I thought at the time that the 90s really sucked from a software perspective. But it's very hard to be, you know, your teenage years always suck. So, you know, how much of this is just like, is kind of too much hormones, too much angst, underdeveloped frontal lobe.
cues.zh: 在八九十年代，年纪越大，我对此就越笃定。我当时觉得，从软件的角度来看，90年代简直糟透了。但这很难说，你知道的，人的青春期总是糟透了。所以，这到底有多少只是因为荷尔蒙过剩、焦虑过度，或者前额叶还没发育好呢？

cues.en: leading you to believe that an era is uniquely bad. But seriously, the 90s were really bad. I think the 90s, they were a dark era for software development, intensely proprietary, more proprietary than the 80s and 70s, actually. It was a local maximum for proprietary software. And so the oral traditions from the 90s are locked up. They existed on these very proprietary islands, even in open source communities, they were locked.
cues.zh: 这会让你误以为那个时代尤其糟糕。但说真的，90年代确实烂透了。我认为90年代是软件开发的黑暗时代，极度封闭且私有，实际上比七八十年代更加封闭。那是专有软件的局部峰值。因此，90年代的口述传统都被封锁起来了。它们存在于这些高度专有的孤岛上，即便在开源社区里，也是被封闭的。

cues.en: Even in the very small open source communities that existed in the 90s, they were still kind of locked away in conferences and so on. That's where the actual kind of oral tradition would happen. There were great collections of oral tradition like SGI.badattitude, anyone who was at SGI at the time, I was never at SGI, but SGI.badattitude had a reputation that went far beyond SGI. Jamie Zawinski actually got a terrific piece.
cues.zh: 哪怕是90年代仅存的极少数开源社区，这类传统也多少被局限在各种会议之类的场合里。那才是真正的口述传统发生的地方。当年有一些很棒的口述传统合集，比如 SGI.badattitude，当时任何在 SGI 工作过的人都知道——我虽然没去过 SGI，但 SGI.badattitude 的声名远播，早已超出了 SGI 的范围。Jamie Zawinski 写过一篇极好的文章，

cues.en: on the Netscape got bad attitude that he created when he went from SGI to Netscape. And then when bad attitude was discovered by management and shut down, he created really bad attitude, a mailing list. And then the true beauty of this, and this means that this document is around somewhere, really bad attitude was discoverable, in discoverable in the legal sense, and was discovered in the Microsoft Netscape case. So Microsoft went through
cues.zh: 是关于他从 SGI 跳槽到 Netscape 后搞的 bad attitude。后来 bad attitude 被管理层发现并关停，他又建了一个名为 really bad attitude 的邮件列表。最妙的是——这也意味着这份文件至今还在某个角落——really bad attitude 在法律意义上是可取证的，并且在微软诉 Netscape 案中被调取了证据。于是微软把

cues.en: really bad attitude. And he's got a very funny line in there. So I guess Microsoft learned that we all complained about the cafeteria food and he can't complain about management all the time. But we had these really great collections of oral tradition, but they've also been lost. And to me, the canonical folklore from this era is an absolutely beautiful piece by a guy named John Brown called The Bug Count Also Rises.
cues.zh: really bad attitude 翻了个底朝天。他在里面写过一句非常搞笑的话。我想微软大概知道了我们都会抱怨食堂的伙食，而且人总不能一直抱怨管理层吧。我们曾拥有这些极好的口述传统合集，但它们也都失传了。对我而言，那个时代的代表性民间故事，是一个叫 John Brown 的人写的一篇绝妙之作，名叫《Bug也升起》。

cues.en: or probably less likely to have read. So actually, if you don't mind, this is going to take me about three minutes, but I would like if I can indulge you.
cues.zh: 或者大家读过的可能性较小。所以说，要是你们不介意的话，大概得占用我三分钟时间，我想占用大家一点时间。

cues.en: I'd like to read this to you. I'll give you a reading. I think that this captures to me the 90s in software. And this is very personal for me because of where I read it, which I'll explain in a second. So this was the winner of a, it was designed to be a Hemingway parody contest, but I believe that this transcends parody and actually becomes as if Hemingway itself, as if Hemingway were describing software development in the 1990s. In the fall of that year,
cues.zh: 我想给大家读一读这段。我来朗读一下。我认为它准确捕捉到了我心中90年代的软件风貌。这对我而言非常私人化，主要是因为我读到它的地点，我稍后会解释。这是一场海明威仿写大赛的冠军作品，但我认为它已经超越了仿写，仿佛就是海明威本人在描写20世纪90年代的软件开发。那年秋天，

cues.en: The rains fell as usual and washed the leaves of the dust and dripped from the leaves on the ground. The shuttles drove through the rainy streets and took the people to meetings. Then later brought them back. Their tires sprang the mist into the air. Many days, he stood for a long time and watched the rain in the shuttles and drank his double-haul mochas. With the mochas, he was strong. Fernando, who worked down the hall and who was large with micro-brews, came to him.
cues.zh: 雨一如既往地下着，洗净了树叶上的尘土，雨滴又顺着叶片落在地上。班车穿行在多雨的街道上，接送人们去开会。随后又把他们送了回来。车轮在空气中扬起层层水汽。好多个日子里，他就这么久久伫立着，看着雨景和班车，喝着他的双份摩卡。有了摩卡，他就充满了力量。顺着走廊走下去、挺着精酿啤酒肚的费尔南多，朝他走了过来。

cues.en: and told him that the chip day was upon them, that the bugs were not yet out. The bugs which were always there, even when you were in cafes, late at night, sipping a red bumper, a double-tall mocha, and you thought you were safe, but they were there. And although Enrico kept the floors slept clean, and the mochas were hot, the bugs were there, and they hated you. When Hernando told him this, he asked how many bugs. The raid is huge with bugs, Hernando said. The bugs are infinite. Why do you ask me?
cues.zh: 并告诉他，芯片日已经迫在眉睫，bug 还没清完。bug 一直都在，哪怕你深夜坐在咖啡馆，啜着一杯红色 bumper、一杯双份高杯摩卡，以为自己安全了，可它们就在那里。尽管 Enrico 把地板保持得一尘不染，摩卡也是热的，bug 还是在那里，而且它们恨你。Hernando 告诉他这些时，他问有多少 bug。Hernando 说，这次行动里 bug 多得吓人。bug 是无限的。你为什么问我？

cues.en: You know, I cannot do this thing anymore with the bugs. Once you were great with the bugs, Fernando said. No one's great at it, he said again. Even Fredo. What a Fredo! Let Fredo fix the bugs, Fernando shrugged. Fredo was finished. He was bored by 3.72s on Chicago. All he does now is drink herb tea and play with his screensavers. Herb Z?
cues.zh: 你知道，我再也没法应付这些 bug 了。Fernando 说，你以前很擅长处理 bug。他又说，没人真的擅长。连 Fredo 也不行。好一个 Fredo！Fernando 耸耸肩：让 Fredo 去修 bug 吧。Fredo 已经完了。他被 Chicago 上的 3.72 秒搞烦了。他现在只喝花草茶、玩屏保。Herb Z？

cues.en: It is true with us. Hernando slugged again. Later he went to his office and sat in the dark for a long time. Then he sent an email to Michaels. Michaels came to him when he was sipping a mocha. They sat silently for a while. Then he asked Michaels, I need you to triage for me. Michaels looks down. I don't do that anymore. He said, this is different. The bugs are worse. Darling, they're the bugs. I'm finished with that.
cues.zh: 我们这边确实如此。Hernando 又猛灌了一口。后来他去了办公室，在黑暗里坐了很久。然后他给 Michaels 发了封邮件。Michaels 来时，他正啜着摩卡。他们沉默地坐了一会儿。然后他问 Michaels：我需要你帮我做分诊。Michaels 低下头：我不再做那个了。他说，这次不一样。bug 更严重了。亲爱的，它们就是 bug。我已经不干那个了。

cues.en: Michael said again. I just wanted him quietly. Had he heard Credo was finished? He was bad with gourd. Now he can only drink herb tea. Herb tea, Michael said? It was true. Michael stood up. And I will do it, my friend. He said formally. I will do it for Credo. Who was once great at the box.
cues.zh: Michael 又说了一遍。我只想让他安静下来。他听说 Credo 已经完了吗？他以前不擅长 gourd。现在他只能喝花草茶。Michael 说，花草茶？这是真的。Michael 站了起来。他说得很正式：我会去做，我的朋友。我会为 Credo 去做。他曾经很擅长 the box。

cues.en: I will do it for the time we filled Prado's office with bouncy balls and for the time Prado wore his Nerf weapons in the marketing hall and slew all of them with no fear and only a great joy at the combat. I will do it for all the people he ate and the bottles of coke we drank. Together they walked slowly back, knowing it would be good as they walked the rain-drip-sulfic malaise and the shoves carried the bodies back from the meetings. So, I think that's amazing.
cues.zh: 我会去做，为了那次我们把 Prado 的办公室塞满弹力球，也为了那次 Prado 戴着他的 Nerf 武器走进市场大厅，毫无畏惧地把他们全干掉，只在战斗中感到巨大的快乐。我会去做，为了他吃掉的所有人，也为了我们喝掉的那些瓶可乐。他们一起慢慢走回去，知道这会很好：他们走过雨水滴答、硫磺般的阴郁，推搡着把尸体从会议里搬回来。所以，我觉得那很了不起。

cues.en: I think that is absolutely amazing. That is closer to me. That is, to me personally, that is actually more relevant than Hemingway. That is, and the reason that this is personal for me, and I wondered where did Quare go? What if Quare actually recognized that? So this was, Roger had this outside his office. So Roger had this taped up outside his office. One of my co-workers had this taped outside his office. And I read this.
cues.zh: 我觉得那绝对了不起。那更贴近我。也就是说，对我个人而言，它其实比 Hemingway 更有意义。也就是说，这件事对我之所以私人，是因为我想知道 Quare 去哪儿了？如果 Quare 真的认出了这一点呢？所以是这样的：Roger 办公室外贴着这个。Roger 把它贴在办公室外面。我的一位同事办公室外也贴着这个。而我读了这个。

cues.en: so many times. This is the thing you would read over and over and over again. And this is what I mean by this is, on the one hand, okay, this is a limb, this is a literary, but this is oral tradition. And the way it was given to me was in oral tradition. This is a senior engineer...
cues.zh: 很多很多次。这就是那种你会一遍又一遍又一遍读的东西。我的意思是，一方面，好吧，这是一段 limb，这是文学性的，但这是口述传统。而它被交给我的方式，就是口述传统。这是一位资深工程师……

cues.en: putting it up outside of his office. And so I absolutely love that. And I think that captures it beautifully. It's very evocative. So fast forward now, if you will, to the dawn of a truly new era, a new era that started actually remarkably recently. So do you recognize this video? How did you watch this video?
cues.zh: 把它贴在他的办公室外面。我真是太喜欢这个了。我觉得它总结得很精妙，非常发人深省。那么现在，请大家随我把时间快进到一个真正新时代的黎明，一个其实离我们非常近的新时代。大家认得这个视频吗？你们看没看过这个视频？

cues.en: And if I were to ask this, of course, we've got some engineer stuff on my team who'd be like, Brian, I was 12 when this came out. I'm like, no, no, that's fine. cues.zh: 因为 C 语言里居然没有逻辑异或，我们有按位异或，但没有逻辑异或，而我们又有逻辑与和逻辑或。我和 Roger Faulkner 经常为此争论不休，Roger Faulkner 就在今年去世了，这也是 Stephen 邀请我来做这次演讲的部分原因，因为我写了纪念 Roger 的文章。Roger 曾是 Solaris 内核开发界的巨擘，随着时间流逝，英雄总会谢幕，但我和 Roger 经常就各种事情争论，我们曾陷入过一场……

cues.en: heated debate over logical XOR because I insisted, I held Dennis in such high regard that I'm just like, they forgot it was a mistake. Roger held in an even higher regard that said anything that is not there is not there intentionally. It is what the founders intended and logical XOR isn't there because it can't short-serve it. And I'm like, Roger, that's stupid.
cues.zh: 关于逻辑异或的激烈争论，因为我坚持认为，我太崇拜 Dennis 了，我觉得他们只是忘了加，这是个疏忽。而 Roger 对他的推崇甚至更上一层楼，他说没加的东西全都是故意不加的。这就是祖师爷的本意，没有逻辑异或，是因为它无法短路。当时我就说，Roger，这太蠢了。

cues.en: That doesn't make sense. Obviously, logical AND can short circuit. Logical OR can short circuit. Logical XOR can't short circuit. But who the hell cares? It's not like there's a commandment that logical operators can short circuit and modules are no. Logical operators, yay, and logical operators shall short circuit. This is ridiculous. And there's no way that that is kind of bad. Logical is like, well, I'll ask that. I'm like,
cues.zh: 这根本说不通。显而易见，逻辑与可以短路。逻辑或可以短路。逻辑异或确实不能短路。但谁在乎啊？又没有哪条戒律规定逻辑运算符就必须能短路，写成什么“逻辑运算符啊，凡逻辑运算符必当短路”。这太荒谬了。绝对不可能因为这种操蛋的理由。Roger 就说，“那好吧，我去问问”。我说，

cues.en: You can ask below. And of course, this is where you get to the underdeveloped frontal lobe. Because I'm like, go ask him. I mean, yeah, ask him now. And so Roger, and much to my chagrin, Roger did go ask him. And again, at this point, this is correspondence from one deceased great to another. So I'm glad we got it.
cues.zh: “你问去呗”。当然，这就是我前额叶还没发育完全的表现。因为我当时就拱火：“你去问他啊！我是说，有种现在就去问！”于是 Roger——让我大跌眼镜的是——Roger 还真去问了。而且现在回想起来，这已经是一位逝去的大师与另一位大师之间的通信了。所以我很庆幸我们留下了记录。

cues.en: Hi Roger, back to communication. Here's a belated response. Logical X4 was omitted because it is of little use, particularly because the shortcut evaluation guaranteed for logical war and logical land doesn't help. Both sides have to be evaluated no matter what. When you do need the effect, A does not equal zero, bitwise X4, B does not equal zero, isn't that much worse than right. Love the Lord.
cues.zh: 嗨 Roger，回到咱们的交流。这是一封迟来的回复。逻辑异或之所以被省略，是因为它没什么用，尤其是逻辑或和逻辑与所保证的短路求值在这里帮不上忙。无论如何两边都必须求值。当你确实需要这个效果时，写成 A != 0 ^ B != 0 也没比直接写差多少。祝好，Dennis。

cues.en: Honestly, part of me was like, this is actually Roger, he's actually just cooking the books on this. He just made this up. I'm like, oh, that's, it is exactly what you said he would say. And it goes through a couple of things. One, it shows that actually, well, one, it shows that original intent to be wrong. But it actually shows that the degree to which people care about your intent.
cues.zh: 老实说，我当时心里有点犯嘀咕：这真是 Roger 写的吗，他是不是在凭空捏造啊？他就是自己编的吧。然后我一想，天哪，这还真跟你说的一模一样。这说明了几件事。第一，它表明最初的意图其实是错的。但它更展现了人们有多在乎你的意图。

cues.en: I actually did care, I mean, to the point like I thought I was going to follow my favor, I really cared about what Dennis thought before I knew he was wrong. But people care what you think. When you write software, people care what you think. Future generations want to honor your intent.
cues.zh: 我当时确实很在意，甚至到了我都觉得自己快偏执的地步了，在知道 Dennis 错了之前，我真的很在乎他是怎么想的。人们其实很在乎你的想法。当你写软件时，人们在乎你是怎么想的。后人是想要尊重你的意图的。

cues.en: And I know it's like, oh, my kids hate me. They think I'm stupid because I can't figure out Snapchat. Well, no, that's not you. Snapchat actually is stupid. And it's very easy to actually kind of denigrate the young as not having veneration for the old. And I am here to say that is not the case. If there's one kind of takeaway of this, I would say that young software engineers
cues.zh: 我知道有人会觉得：“唉，我的孩子嫌弃我，他们觉得我很笨，因为我玩不明白 Snapchat。” 哎，真不是你的问题，Snapchat 本来就很蠢。人们很容易去贬低年轻人，觉得他们不尊重前辈。但我今天想说，事实并非如此。如果说这件事能给大家什么启发的话，那就是年轻的软件工程师——

cues.en: As I was, when I was doing this, you probably were young, look to better rate older software engineers. They want to do right by them. They want to understand, help me understand your intent so I can abide by it. It's important to them. So we need to tell them what our intent was. You know, one of the major failings, I mean, JavaScript, as I said before, JavaScript is the failed state of programming languages.
cues.zh: 就像当年的我一样，我干这事时还很年轻，年轻人都很想去尊崇资深的软件工程师。他们想要顺应前辈的思路。他们想说：“帮我理解你的意图吧，这样我才能遵循它。” 这对他们很重要。所以我们需要告诉他们我们的意图是什么。你知道，一个重大的失败案例——我是说 JavaScript，正如我之前说的，JavaScript 就是编程语言界的“失败国家”。

cues.en: One of the reasons that that is true is there is no constitution to JavaScript. There is Brendan Eich never wrote a book. Oops. Where's the book, Brendan? You let other people write about your programming language. No one knows what your intent is. You need to broadcast that intent. So your intent's important.
cues.zh: 之所以会这样，原因之一就是 JavaScript 根本没有“宪法”。Brendan Eich 从来没写过一本书。哎呀，书呢，Brendan？你让别人去写关于你这门编程语言的书。根本没人知道你的意图是什么。你必须把这种意图传达出来。所以，你的意图至关重要。

cues.en: And the final one, which is not worth belaboring, because I belabor it, trust me to death, in a chapter I wrote in beautiful code, but is a comment that Jeff Onwick and I wrote together in a moment of total crisis when we had a bug that actually looked like we could not fix.
cues.zh: 最后一个例子就不多赘述了，因为我在《Beautiful Code》里写的那一章里已经讲得够透彻了，相信我，真的讲烂了；那是 Jeff Bonwick 和我在一次彻底的危机时刻共同写下的一段注释，当时遇到了一个看起来根本修不好的 bug。

cues.en: Which is something. Jeff and I have both fixed a lot of bugs, and we thought we had met our match. And we had, both of us have referred to as the mind meld, and had an extremely intense week where we tried to resolve this, a bug in someone else's code. And when we finally found a path, there was this very narrow path by which we could solve this problem.
cues.zh: 这可非同小可。Jeff 和我都修过无数的 bug，但那次我们觉得真的遇到对手了。我们俩后来都把这称为“心灵感应”，我们度过了极其紧张的一周，拼尽全力去解决别人代码里的一个 bug。当我们终于找到一条出路时，那是一条极其狭窄、勉强能帮我们解决问题的绝径。

cues.en: it felt like we had taken a bit of a kind of a cheesy solution, but we knew it was the only one. And Jeff did something which I will always thank him for, which is in this long explanation of what we did, he added this, you think this is cheesy? Let's see you do better. And this is a little note to future generations that like,
cues.zh: 感觉我们像是用了一个有点凑合的方案，但我们知道这是唯一的解法。Jeff 做了一件让我永远感激的事，在这段对我们所作所为的长篇解释中，他加上了这句：“你觉得这很凑合？有本事你来写个更好的。”这是留给后人的一张小纸条，

cues.en: It's like, yeah, we get it. We get it. This doesn't feel really elegant. But we've suffered. We've suffered. The scar tissue is right here. Let me show you the scar, young sir. But before you throw yourself on this machinery to improve it, understand what we've done before. And it's been almost 15 years since we wrote that, more. Almost 20 years since we wrote that, no one's done better. And I don't think anyone ever will. That code will survive forever.
cues.zh: 就像在说：“行，我们懂，我们懂。这看起来确实不太优雅。但我们吃过苦头，真的吃过。伤疤就在这儿呢。年轻人，让我给你看看这道疤。但在你扑到这台机器上试图改进它之前，先明白我们之前都经历了什么。”我们写下那段代码距今快 15 年了，不，甚至快 20 年了，还没人能做得更好。我觉得以后也不会有。那段代码会永远存活下去。

cues.en: So I think this kind of brings me to the thrust of this, which I think code comments are oral tradition. And if you look at the best comments, the best comments have this aspect of oral tradition too. They explain not only what's going on, but they give you a narrative as to why. Why is this happening? Why are we doing this? Why are we solving this problem? Why are we here? And that comments live with the code but don't affect its correctness?
cues.zh: 所以我想这引出了我的核心观点：我认为代码注释就是口述传统。如果你去看看那些最棒的注释，它们都有这种口述传统的特质。它们不仅解释了代码在做什么，还向你讲述了背后的缘由。为什么会这样？我们为什么这么做？为什么要解决这个问题？我们为什么会在这里？而且注释与代码共存，却不影响其正确性？

cues.en: Oh my god, that's great. We, as software engineers, get this free body of literature that we get to tuck in with our code. That is an incredible power that we don't use often enough. We don't use this often enough. And we get broad scope and artistic license in our comments.
cues.zh: 天哪，这太棒了。作为软件工程师，我们平白得到了这样一片可以塞进代码里的文学天地。这是一项我们用得还不够频繁的强大能力。我们真的用得太少了。而且我们在注释中拥有极大的发挥空间和艺术自由。

cues.en: Now, Theo would be right to twitch right now, because when I say artistic license, I do mean within reason. And Larry Wall, if you're listening, putting Elphin in a comment is wrong. And if you see Theo Shostak, oh, one of you is violating the others restraining order. So it's broad artistic license, but not overly broad. But it does allow us
cues.zh: 现在 Theo 听到这儿肯定得眼角抽搐了，因为当我说艺术自由时，确实是指在合理范围内的。Larry Wall，如果你在听的话，把精灵语写在注释里是不对的。要是你碰到了 Theo Shostak，哦，那你们俩肯定有人违反了限制令。所以这是广阔的艺术自由，但也不能太离谱。但这确实允许我们

cues.en: to convey that intent, explain what we're doing, because these software systems are going to survive long past us when we write, write for future generations, write software for the next hundred years. And I don't say this in jest. I look at how much code, I mean, I'm a relatively young person, we are young people. I look at code that I've written in my career that is running unperturbed from 20 years ago.
cues.zh: 去传达那种意图，解释我们正在做的事情，因为这些软件系统的寿命会远超我们自己。当我们敲下代码时，是在为后人而写，是在为未来的一百年编写软件。我可不是在开玩笑。我看看那些代码——我是说，我还算年轻，我们都还年轻。我看着自己职业生涯中写的代码，从 20 年前一直平静地运行至今。

cues.en: And his show is not in a trajectory to go anywhere. This stuff will survive for a long time. Comments are how we speak to future generations. And it is very important that we use this incredible power. They are the art within this timeless machine. I mean, it is this amazing, amazing power. So, just to wrap up, and I'm sorry I'm going a little over here, but the sovereign sharing has changed
cues.zh: 而且迹象表明它根本没有被取代的势头。这些东西会存活很久很久。注释正是我们与后人对话的方式。善用这种不可思议的力量至关重要。它们是这台永恒机器中的艺术品。我是说，这真是一项了不起的强大能力。所以最后总结一下，抱歉我有点超时了，但软件工程在过去十年里

cues.en: Incredibly in the last decade. We have seen it's not just the rise of YouTube it is I mean we are in the open source era and I mean Steven's been talking about this for a long time But it's only really been in the last five six years that we have been in an all open era It's amazing. Everything is open transparent distributed. It's a revolution or tradition and we're recording this stuff. We've got oral literature I mean, it's it you know, if you've given a presentation your kids will watch it
cues.zh: 发生了不可思议的改变。我们看到的不仅是 YouTube 的崛起，我是说，我们身处开源时代，Steven 已经谈论这个很久了，但真正进入全开源时代，其实也就是最近五六年的事。这太不可思议了。一切都是开放、透明、分布式的。这是一场口述传统的革命，我们正在记录这些东西。我们拥有了口述文学。我是说，如果你做过一场演讲，你的孩子会看，

cues.en: your grandchildren will watch it, your great-grandchildren will watch it. And it changes the way you think about what you're doing and the longevity of it. And again, we can expose that why of the thing. And I would say if you're a software engineer, you've got a team of software engineers, encourage folks to record the oral tradition. Because record the things that you don't otherwise record.
cues.zh: 你的孙辈会看，你的重孙辈也会看。这改变了你对自己所做之事及其生命周期的看法。再次强调，我们可以展现出事情背后的“为什么”。我想说，如果你是一名软件工程师，或者你带了一支软件工程师团队，去鼓励大家记录下这种口述传统吧。去记录那些在其他地方根本不会被记录下来的东西。

cues.en: in comments where appropriate, in a video where appropriate, but record these things, and not just for future generations, but also because it allows a source base to project its values. Here's who we're about. When people want to come work for Joyant, I have them go watch a couple of key videos just so they know what they're getting themselves into. And as I tell people, like, I've got a couple of videos, and if you know me, you know which ones I'm referring to, I'm like, you will watch this, and you will want to work here more or less.
cues.zh: 合适的地方写进注释，合适的地方录成视频，但一定要记录下来；这不仅是留给后人，更是为了让代码库展现它的价值观。这就是我们这群人。当有人想来 Joyent 工作时，我会让他们先去看几个核心视频，好让他们清楚自己将要面对什么。正如我对大家说的，我有这么几个视频——如果你了解我，就知道我指的是哪些——我会说，你看完之后，想来这里工作的意愿或多或少会有所改变。

cues.en: But you will not want to work here the same after you watch this video. But by doing that, you allow people to opt in to your traditions, your values. And it leads to much more success in hiring. You get a much more diverse team. You get people you wouldn't otherwise get. Because the values that you have transcend the traditional ways that you hire people.
cues.zh: 看完这个视频后，你的想法绝不可能和之前一样。但这样做，能让人们主动认同你的传统和价值观。这会让招聘变得成功得多。你会得到一个更加多元化的团队，招到那些原本不可能招到的人。因为你所秉持的价值观，已经超越了传统的招聘方式。

cues.en: And I think our oral tradition is our legacy to future generations and we owe it to those generations to expand on. Thank you very much.
cues.zh: 我认为，我们的口述传统就是留给后人的宝贵遗产，而把它发扬光大，是我们对后人应尽的责任。非常感谢大家。
